One-Way ANOVA — Homework 6 Solved

Course 2.1 · Methods & Statistics · Bruno Bocanegra

Prepared for Sezen18 solved questions50 practice questions44 flashcards

Learning objectives

By the end of this page you should be able to do all eight of these without having to think about which one you are doing.

  • Name the factor, its levels and the dependent variable, and say whether ANOVA or a t test fits.
  • Produce every degree of freedom in the table from just N and k, and check them by addition.
  • Build SS Between and SS Within from group means, sizes and standard deviations.
  • Complete an ANOVA table in either direction, and read F out of it.
  • State H₀ and Hₐ in the fixed ANOVA form, and turn a p-value into a modest conclusion.
  • Compute and interpret R² (eta-squared) as the share of variance the factor explains.
  • Explain why post-hoc tests need a corrected alpha, and run pairwise comparisons against an MSD.
  • Tell a Type I error from a Type II error, and say when a causal claim is allowed.

The method: symptom → diagnosis → treatment

When you cannot tell what a question is asking, here is what is actually happening: you are reading the words and hunting for a formula at the same time. That never works. It is not a failure of ability — it is a missing step in the middle.

A doctor never does that. Nobody looks at a patient and reaches straight for a prescription. They take the symptoms, they name the diagnosis, and only then does the treatment follow. And that is the crucial part: once you have the diagnosis, the treatment is not a decision any more. It is already written down.

One-way ANOVA has exactly eight diagnoses. Every question in this homework is one of them, and each one has a single fixed procedure. So the whole skill is step ②, and it takes about five seconds.

The test of whether you have really diagnosed

You should be able to say the case type out loud BEFORE you look at the answer options at all. If you cannot, do not look at them yet — a well-written wrong option is designed to look right to someone who skipped step ②.

The eight diagnoses

Every question in this homework, and on the exam, is one of these eight. Find the card whose words match the question, then follow its procedure.

1Name the design

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “The factor in this study is…” · “the levels of the factor are…”
  • “The dependent variable is…” · “how many groups?”
  • “Should this be analysed with a t test or an ANOVA?”
③ Treatment — every time
  1. Find the DEPENDENT variable first: the thing measured on each person. Always quantitative.
  2. The FACTOR is the qualitative variable saying which group you are in.
  3. The LEVELS are its categories. Count them: that is k. Count all the scores: that is N.
  4. Two groups → a t test will do. Three or more → ANOVA. And for two groups, F = t².
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 8 — what you may conclude. Type 1 asks what the variables ARE (fixed before any data arrive); type 8 asks what the results MEAN.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Counting the factor as a level, or the levels as separate factors. ONE factor with THREE levels — not three factors. And the dependent variable is never a level.

2Degrees of freedom

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “The degrees of freedom for the F test are…”
  • “…between / within / total” · “df for error”
  • Or hidden inside another question: you cannot look up a critical F without them.
③ Treatment — every time
  1. Find N (all the scores) and k (the number of groups).
  2. df Between = k − 1. This is the numerator df of F.
  3. df Within = N − k. This is the denominator df, and the one every post-hoc test uses.
  4. df Total = N − 1.
  5. Check: (k − 1) + (N − k) = N − 1. If they do not add, one of them is wrong.
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 4 — fill in the table. Type 2 asks for a degree of freedom as the ANSWER; type 4 is bookkeeping inside a table, where a df is only a step on the way to an MS or an F — whether it is printed for you or has to be recovered from the text.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Writing k for the between df (off by one) or N − 1 for the within df (off by k − 1). Both look plausible and both are offered as options.

3Build the sums of squares

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “Compute SS Between” — with group means and sizes given
  • “What is SS Total / SS Error?” — with the other two given
  • A summary table of n, mean and standard deviation per group, and no ANOVA table
③ Treatment — every time
  1. SS Between = Σ [ nᵢ × (group mean − overall mean)² ]. One term per group, then add.
  2. SS Within = Σ (score − its own group mean)². From summary data: Σ (nᵢ − 1) sᵢ².
  3. SS Total = Σ (score − overall mean)².
  4. And the shortcut that answers most exam versions: SS Total = SS Between + SS Within. Given any two, the third is one subtraction away.
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 4 — fill in the table. Type 3 hands you means and sizes and asks you to BUILD the sums of squares; type 4 hands you a table with gaps.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Forgetting the group size in SS Between, and forgetting the −1 in SS Within. Each squared deviation of a group mean is weighted by how many people are in that group.

4Fill in the ANOVA table

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “The value of MS Between / MS Within is…”
  • “Complete the following ANOVA table” · any table printed with ** or blanks
  • “Given MS Within and the group sizes, what is SS Within?”
③ Treatment — every time
  1. SS and df ADD down the table: SS Between + SS Within = SS Total.
  2. MS = SS ÷ df, always on the SAME row. Never cross rows.
  3. F = MS Between ÷ MS Within.
  4. Backwards is the same rules rearranged: SS = MS × df, and df Within = N − k recovers N.
  5. Two more come free: R² = SS Between ÷ SS Total, and sₚ = √(MS Within).
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 2 — degrees of freedom. A table is mostly df, so type-2 instincts fire; but type 4 is bookkeeping, not derivation.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Dividing SS Between by SS Within to get F. F is a ratio of MEAN squares — you must convert both first, and that conversion needs the df.

5Test it: F, the table, the decision

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “The value of the F statistic is…” · “reject H₀ if F > …”
  • “What do you conclude at α = .05?” · “what does p = 0.001 mean?”
  • “State the null and alternative hypotheses”
③ Treatment — every time
  1. The hypotheses never change. H₀: all population means equal. Hₐ: AT LEAST ONE differs. Never directional, never “all differ”.
  2. F = MS Between ÷ MS Within. Under H₀ it should be around 1.
  3. Enter the F table with the PAIR (df Between, df Within) at your α. If your exact df row is missing, drop to the next LOWER df — the cautious direction.
  4. Reject H₀ when observed F is LARGER than the critical value, or equivalently when p < α.
  5. Write the conclusion about the POPULATION, and keep it modest.
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 6 — effect size. Type 5 asks WHETHER there is a difference; type 6 asks HOW BIG. A tiny difference can be significant in a big sample, so you need both.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Writing Hₐ as “all the means are different”, or comparing p with .05 when the question gave you a different α.

6Effect size: R² (eta-squared)

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “What proportion of the variance is explained by the factor?”
  • “R²” · “eta-squared” · “how strong is the relationship?”
  • Any question that reports a significant F and then asks how much it matters
③ Treatment — every time
  1. R² = SS Between ÷ SS TOTAL. The denominator is always the total, never SS Within.
  2. It runs from 0 to 1 and is a proportion of the variance in the dependent variable.
  3. Say it in a sentence: “X% of the variation in [the score] is explained by [the factor].”
  4. In this course, R² above about .20 is called a strong effect.
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 5 — the F test. Both come from the same table and both go in the conclusion, but they answer different questions.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Dividing SS Between by SS Within, or quoting R² as evidence of significance. The two travel together but answer different questions: a real effect can be small, and a large effect in a small sample can miss significance, because p depends on effect size AND sample size.

7After the test: which pairs differ?

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “Which pairs of means are significantly different?”
  • “Why can we not simply do three t tests?” · “Bonferroni” · “Tukey” · “post-hoc”
  • “What is the adjusted alpha per test?” · “how many comparisons?”
③ Treatment — every time
  1. First check you are allowed to be here: in this course, post-hoc tests are run only after a SIGNIFICANT F.
  2. The problem: each test risks 5%, so across several the family-wise risk climbs (three tests at .05 leave only about 86% chance of no false alarm, if they were independent).
  3. Bonferroni splits alpha: α per test = α ÷ (number of tests).
  4. Number of pairs for k groups = k(k − 1)/2.
  5. All of these use the pooled sₚ = √(MS Within) with df = df Within — which is why the ANOVA has to come first.
  6. If an MSD is given, the work is subtraction: compare each pair’s gap with it.
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 5 — the F test. They are two halves of the same analysis. Type 5 is the OVERALL test; type 7 is the follow-up. If the question names specific groups, it is type 7.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Thinking the correction makes the test better. It makes it HARDER, deliberately — that is the price of not fooling yourself.

8What you may conclude — and which error you may have made

① Symptom — what the words look like
  • “Which assumptions must hold for this ANOVA to be valid?”
  • “Can we conclude that the factor CAUSED the difference?”
  • “A Type I / Type II error here would be…” · “which statement is FALSE?”
③ Treatment — every time
  1. The three assumptions, every time: the population scores are Normally distributed; the groups have EQUAL variances in the population; the observations are independent.
  2. Check equal variances with the rule of thumb: largest s ≤ 2 × smallest s.
  3. For causality, ask two questions: was the factor MANIPULATED, and were people RANDOMLY ASSIGNED? Both yes → a causal claim is allowed. If people arrived already in their groups, it is observational and no F however large licenses causality.
  4. Type I error: you REJECTED a true H₀ — a false alarm, probability α. Type II error: you FAILED to reject a false H₀ — a missed difference, probability β.
  5. Read every error option in two halves: what you CONCLUDED, and what was true “when in fact…”.
  6. Keep the conclusion modest: at least one population mean differs. Not all, not which one.
Differential — the type this gets confused with
Type 1 — name the design. Both are word questions about the design rather than the numbers. Type 1 asks what the variables ARE; type 8 asks what the results MEAN.
⚠ The mis-diagnosis
Reading “equal variances” as a claim about the SAMPLES. The assumption is about the populations; the sample variances are only the evidence you judge it by.

What F is actually comparing

If H₀ is true and all the population means really are equal, the sample means still will not land on top of each other — sampling noise alone scatters them. So between-group spread is never zero, not even when nothing is going on. The question is whether the means are FURTHER apart than noise alone would put them, and that comparison is a ratio: F = MS Between ÷ MS Within.

Key terms — read these first

FactorThe qualitative (categorical) variable that says which group someone is in. The independent variable. One-way ANOVA has exactly one.
LevelsThe categories of the factor. How many there are is k.
Dependent variableThe quantitative thing measured on each person — the score. One number per participant.
N and kN is how many scores in total; k is how many groups. Every degree of freedom in this lecture comes from these two numbers.
SS BetweenΣ nᵢ(group mean − overall mean)². The variation in the group MEANS — the systematic part, what the factor explains.
SS Within (= SS Error)Σ(score − its own group mean)², which equals Σ(nᵢ − 1)sᵢ² when you have summary data. The noise: individual differences inside the groups.
Mean square (MS)A sum of squares divided by its OWN degrees of freedom. This is what makes the between and within pieces comparable.
F statisticMS Between ÷ MS Within. Around 1 when H₀ is true; well above 1 when the means are further apart than the noise explains.
H₀ and HₐH₀: all the population means are equal. Hₐ: at least one differs. Never directional, never “all differ”.
p-valueThe probability of an F this large or larger IF H₀ were true. Small p → reject H₀.
R² (eta-squared)SS Between ÷ SS Total. The share of the total variation the factor accounts for. A size, not a significance.
Pooled standard deviation sₚ√(MS Within). The one spread shared by all the groups, under the equal-variance assumption. Every post-hoc comparison is built on it.
Family-wise error rateThe chance of at least one false positive across a whole set of comparisons. It climbs as you add tests — which is why Bonferroni and Tukey exist.
Bonferroni correctionDivide α by the number of comparisons. Makes each test stricter so the family-wise rate is held to at most α — deliberately cautious.
Minimum significant difference (MSD)The yardstick a post-hoc method produces. Two group means differ if the gap between them exceeds it.
Type I / Type II errorType I: rejecting a TRUE H₀ — a false alarm, probability α. Type II: failing to reject a FALSE H₀ — a missed difference, probability β.

How to use this page

Work through it in this order. Read the Overview once, properly — especially the eight case types. Then open the homework questions one at a time and, before you read my walkthrough, say out loud which case type it is. That guess is the thing being trained; everything after it is arithmetic.

The two practice exams hide their answers until you commit. Do exam A, retry whatever you missed, and leave exam B for a few days later — spacing them out is worth more than doing both tonight.

Case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
Assume you have computed an analysis of variance for three groups with 10 observations per group. The degrees of freedom for the F test are:
›
  • a.3 and 30
  • b.2 and 10
  • c.2 and 27
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
You are told how many groups there are and how many people are in each. Nothing else. The question wants the PAIR of degrees of freedom that an F test is looked up with.
② Diagnosis
Case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Find k, the number of groups. Three groups, so k = 3.
  2. Find N, the number of scores in total. Ten per group across three groups, so N = 3 × 10 = 30. Notice that N is people, not groups — this is where most of the lost marks live.
  3. df between (the numerator) = k − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2.
  4. df within (the denominator) = N − k = 30 − 3 = 27.
  5. Check: 2 + 27 = 29, and N − 1 = 29. ✓
✓ Answer: c. 2 and 27.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. Uses k instead of k − 1 on top, and N instead of N − k underneath. Both halves are the raw counts with no subtraction — it is what you write if you have not yet learned that df always costs you something.
✗b. Gets the numerator right and then uses the GROUP size (10) instead of N − k for the denominator. This is the single most common ANOVA df error: the denominator is built from everyone in the study, not from one group.
✓c. Correct. k − 1 = 2 on top, N − k = 27 underneath, and they add to N − 1 = 29.
Carry this forward
Write “N = ___, k = ___” at the top of your working before you do anything else. Every degree of freedom in this entire lecture comes out of those two numbers.
2
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
Assume you have computed an analysis of variance F test and obtained a P-value, p = 0.001. This means that:
›
  • a.all the groups have the same mean
  • b.all the group means are different
  • c.some of the group means differ from the others
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
You are given a p-value and asked what it entitles you to SAY. No arithmetic. This is really a question about how modest the ANOVA conclusion has to be.
② Diagnosis
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. p = 0.001 is smaller than any usual α (.05, .01), so you reject H₀.
  2. Write down what H₀ actually claimed: all the population means are equal.
  3. Rejecting that claim means it is NOT true that all the means are equal. Say that out loud — the opposite of “all equal” is “not all equal”, which is the same as “at least one differs”.
  4. It is not “all differ”. One group out of ten being different is already enough to make “all equal” false, and the F test cannot tell the difference between those two situations.
✓ Answer: c. some of the group means differ from the others.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. This is what you would conclude if p were LARGE. And even then you would not claim the means are the same — you would only say you found no evidence that they differ.
✗b. Too strong. A significant F says the “all equal” picture is wrong; it never says every group is different from every other. Spotting this over-claim is worth easy marks.
✓c. Correct. “Not all equal” = at least one group mean sits apart from the others. Which one, F does not say — that is what the post-hoc tests are for.
Carry this forward
The alternative hypothesis in ANOVA is always “at least one differs”, never “all differ”. Any option that says all of them differ is wrong before you read the rest.
3
Case type 1 · Name the design
An ANOVA F test is an extension of a:
›
  • a.two-sample t test
  • b.two-sample z test
  • c.two-sample test of proportions
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
Which two-group test does ANOVA generalise? Pure design knowledge — the question is asking what kind of data ANOVA handles.
② Diagnosis
Case type 1 · Name the design
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Ask what ANOVA needs: a QUANTITATIVE dependent variable, and a QUALITATIVE factor that says which group you are in.
  2. Now find the two-group test with exactly those ingredients. The two-sample t test compares the MEANS of a quantitative variable across two groups. Same ingredients, two groups instead of three or more.
  3. The link is exact, not loose: with k = 2 groups the pooled (equal-variance) t test and the F test give the same decision, and F = t². That identity is in the lecture and is worth remembering.
✓ Answer: a. two-sample t test.
Why each option is what it is
✓a. Correct. Same quantitative DV, same qualitative grouping variable, just more than two groups. And for exactly two groups, F = t² against the pooled t test.
✗b. A z test for means needs the POPULATION standard deviation to be known, which it almost never is. ANOVA estimates the spread from the data itself (that is what MS Within is), so the t family is the right relative.
✗c. A test of proportions compares percentages — a CATEGORICAL outcome, like yes/no. ANOVA compares means of a quantitative outcome. Wrong kind of dependent variable entirely.
Carry this forward
ANOVA = t test with more than two groups. If you can see which two-group test an option is describing, you can see immediately whether its dependent variable matches.
4
Case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
I have three groups for which I want to perform an ANOVA. They have standard deviations s₁ = 2.5, s₂ = 3.4, s₃ = 6.4, and the plots of the data indicate all samples are approximately Normal with no outliers. Is the ANOVA appropriate?
›
  • a.Yes
  • b.No
  • c.Not enough information to tell
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
You are handed the three sample standard deviations and told the shapes look Normal. The question is whether the ANOVA assumptions survive. Normality has already been handed to you — so the question is really about the OTHER assumption.
② Diagnosis
Case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. List the three assumptions: Normal populations, EQUAL population variances, independent observations.
  2. Normality: the question tells you the plots look approximately Normal with no outliers. That one is satisfied, and the question says so on purpose, to make you look elsewhere.
  3. Equal variances: you cannot check the populations, so you check the samples. The rule of thumb used in this course: the ANOVA is safe if the LARGEST standard deviation is no more than TWICE the smallest.
  4. Largest s = 6.4, smallest s = 2.5. Twice the smallest is 5.0, and 6.4 > 5.0. (Equivalently 6.4 ÷ 2.5 = 2.56, which is bigger than 2.)
  5. The equal-variance assumption fails, so the ANOVA is not appropriate here.
✓ Answer: b. No.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. What you answer if you check only the assumption the question spoon-feeds you. Normality is fine; the variances are not.
✓b. Correct. 6.4 is more than twice 2.5, so the equal-variance assumption is violated and the ANOVA should not be used as it stands.
✗c. You have everything you need: three standard deviations and a statement about shape. This option is only tempting if you do not know the rule of thumb to apply.
Carry this forward
Largest s ≤ 2 × smallest s settles the equal-variance half of “is the ANOVA appropriate?”, and the question hands you the standard deviations precisely so you can apply it. Normality and independence are the other two halves — usually given to you in words, as they are here.
5
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
A manufacturer is running an experiment using the standard (control) infant formula, and two new formulas, A and B. 120 infants are randomly assigned to three groups (40 per group) and the study runs for 12 weeks. The variable measured is Total IGA (mg/dl), with higher values more desirable. A one-way ANOVA is employed. The hypotheses tested by the one-way ANOVA F test are:
›
  • a.H₀: the mean IGA score is the same for all three formulas. Hₐ: the mean IGA score is HIGHER for both treatment groups A and B than the control group.
  • b.H₀: the mean IGA score is the same for all three formulas. Hₐ: the mean IGA score is HIGHER for at least one of the two treatment groups than the control.
  • c.H₀: the mean IGA score is the same for all three formulas. Hₐ: the mean IGA score is NOT the same for all three formulas.
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
All three options give the same H₀, so H₀ is not what is being tested here — the question is purely about Hₐ. Everything about infants, weeks and milligrams is scenery.
② Diagnosis
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Cover the H₀ line in all three options. They are identical. So the only thing that can make an option wrong is its Hₐ.
  2. Recall the fixed form of the ANOVA alternative: at least one population mean differs from the others. Nothing about direction, nothing about which group.
  3. Now test each Hₐ against that form. Does it name a direction (higher, lower)? Then it is not the ANOVA alternative: squaring the distances throws the sign away, so there is no direction left for F to test. (F itself is still looked up in the upper tail — it is the ALTERNATIVE that has no direction, not the table.)
  4. Only the third option says “not the same”, with no direction and no named group.
✓ Answer: c. Hₐ: the mean IGA score is not the same for all three formulas.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. Two faults at once: it is directional (“higher”) and it demands that BOTH new formulas beat the control. That is a much narrower claim than F ever tests.
✗b. Still directional. “Higher for at least one” is the right shape for a one-sided follow-up comparison, but F cannot test a direction — this is the trap option, and it is designed to look right because “at least one” sounds familiar.
✓c. Correct. No direction, no particular group: just the flat denial of H₀.
Carry this forward
When every option shares the same H₀, stop reading H₀. And strike out any Hₐ that uses the word higher, lower, better or worse — the ANOVA F test has no direction.

Case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
A realtor wishes to assess whether a difference exists between home prices in three subdivisions. Independent samples of homes from each subdivision are obtained and their prices recorded. What is the value of the degrees of freedom for Groups?
›
SourceDFSSMSF
Groups
Error15253.50
Total410.94
  • a.2
  • b.3
  • c.14
  • d.15
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
An ANOVA table with most of it missing, and the question wants the Groups degrees of freedom. The table does not tell you N — but the scenario tells you k.
② Diagnosis
Case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Read the scenario for k, not the table: THREE subdivisions, so k = 3.
  2. df Groups = k − 1 = 3 − 1 = 2. That is the whole question.
  3. Worth doing once, because the next two questions need it: df Total = df Groups + df Error = 2 + 15 = 17, so N = 18 homes altogether. (How they split between the three subdivisions is not stated, and nothing here needs it.)
✓ Answer: a. 2.
Why each option is what it is
✓a. Correct. Three groups, so k − 1 = 2.
✗b. The number of groups itself, with the subtraction forgotten. Always one too many.
✗c. df Error − 1, that is 15 − 1. No rule anywhere in ANOVA subtracts one from a df that has already been computed. Numbers sitting near the real ones are not evidence; the rule is.
✗d. The Error df, copied from the row above. Tempting when a table is mostly blank and one real number is sitting there.
Carry this forward
When an ANOVA table has gaps, the scenario usually carries the number the table is missing. “Three subdivisions”, “three formulas”, “three fitness levels” — that is k, and it is doing real work.
7
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
Referring to the same realtor table: what is the value of the MSG (the mean square for Groups)?
›
SourceDFSSMSF
Groups2??
Error15253.50
Total17410.94
  • a.16.90
  • b.78.72
  • c.157.44
  • d.253.50
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
Complete one cell of the table. MS always means “a sum of squares divided by its own degrees of freedom”, so you need SS Groups first — and SS Groups is not printed.
② Diagnosis
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Get SS Groups by subtraction, because SS adds DOWN the column: SS Total = SS Groups + SS Error.
  2. SS Groups = 410.94 − 253.50 = 157.44.
  3. Now divide across the row by that row’s own df: MSG = SS Groups ÷ df Groups = 157.44 ÷ 2.
  4. MSG = 78.72.
✓ Answer: b. 78.72.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. This is MSE, the mean square for Error: 253.50 ÷ 15 = 16.90. The right operation on the wrong row. (Keep it — question 8 needs it.)
✓b. Correct. 157.44 ÷ 2 = 78.72.
✗c. This is SS Groups, the step before. You found the sum of squares and then forgot to divide by the degrees of freedom — which is exactly the step that turns a sum into a mean.
✗d. SS Error, copied straight from the table. A number that is printed is rarely the answer to a “what is the value of…” question.
Carry this forward
SS adds DOWN the column; MS = SS ÷ df ACROSS the row. Every missing cell in an ANOVA table falls to one of those two moves.
8
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
Referring to the same realtor table: what is the value of the F statistic?
›
SourceDFSSMSF
Groups2157.4478.72?
Error15253.5016.90
Total17410.94
  • a.0.21
  • b.1.13
  • c.4.66
  • d.39.36
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
The last cell. F is always the same ratio, and both ingredients are now in the table.
② Diagnosis
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. MSE = SS Error ÷ df Error = 253.50 ÷ 15 = 16.90.
  2. F = MS Groups ÷ MS Error = 78.72 ÷ 16.90.
  3. F = 4.658, which rounds to 4.66.
  4. Sanity check: F is comfortably bigger than 1, so the group means are further apart than the noise inside the groups would explain. That is the direction you expect when something real is going on.
✓ Answer: c. 4.66.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. The ratio upside down: 16.90 ÷ 78.72 = 0.215. F always has the BETWEEN mean square on top — the systematic piece over the noise, never the other way round.
✗b. MS Error ÷ df Error: 16.90 ÷ 15 = 1.13 — the Error row divided by its degrees of freedom TWICE. Once you have a mean square the df has already been used; it does not get used again.
✓c. Correct. 78.72 ÷ 16.90 = 4.66.
✗d. MS Groups ÷ df Groups: 78.72 ÷ 2 = 39.36 — the Groups row divided by its df twice, the same slip as option a but on the other row.
Carry this forward
F = MS Between ÷ MS Within. If your F comes out below 1 when the question clearly wants a significant result, you have almost certainly inverted the ratio.
9
Case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
One reason we use the Bonferroni or Tukey method for multiple comparisons is that:
›
  • a.as we perform more comparisons, the family-wise α rate increases
  • b.the individual comparisons are not independent
  • c.neither (a) nor (b)
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
Why do we correct at all? The question is asking for the PROBLEM that the correction was invented to solve.
② Diagnosis
Case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Start from one test. A single t test at α = .05 has a 5% chance of a false alarm, so a 95% chance of behaving.
  2. Now do three of them. If they behaved independently, the chance of getting all three right would be 0.95 × 0.95 × 0.95 = 0.857 — about 86%. So the chance of at least one false alarm has climbed from 5% to roughly 14%.
  3. That climbing risk across the whole FAMILY of comparisons is what “family-wise error rate” names, and it is what Bonferroni and Tukey hold down.
  4. Bonferroni’s fix is blunt and easy to remember: divide α by the number of tests, so each individual test runs at a stricter level and the family-wise rate is held to AT MOST 5%. At most, not exactly — Bonferroni is deliberately cautious.
✓ Answer: a. as we perform more comparisons, the family-wise α rate increases.
Why each option is what it is
✓a. Correct. More comparisons, more chances to be fooled — that is the problem the correction exists for.
✗b. It is true that pairwise comparisons share the same data and so are not independent, which is why Tukey is cleverer than Bonferroni. But it is not the REASON the methods exist. The reason is the inflating error rate; the dependence is a detail of how you fix it.
✗c. Wrong because (a) is a correct and sufficient reason on its own.
Carry this forward
Bonferroni does not make the test better — it makes it HARDER, deliberately. You are paying in power to stop the false-alarm rate rising with the number of pairs.
10
Case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
One-way ANOVA is applied to independent random samples from three Normally distributed populations with equal variances. The error sum of squares is equal to:
›
What you are given
  • Group 1 — n₁ = 8, x̄₁ = 15, s₁ = 2
  • Group 2 — n₂ = 10, x̄₂ = 18, s₂ = 3
  • Group 3 — n₃ = 8, x̄₃ = 20, s₃ = 2
  • a.137
  • b.55
  • c.154
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
“Error sum of squares” is another name for SS Within. You are given group sizes, means and standard deviations — and no raw scores, so there is a formula for exactly this.
② Diagnosis
Case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Recognise the vocabulary first: error = within. SS Error and SS Within are the same quantity under two names, and exams switch between them freely.
  2. With raw scores you would compute Σ(score − its own group mean)². You do not have raw scores. The version for summary data is SS Within = Σ (nᵢ − 1) sᵢ².
  3. Notice that the MEANS are not used at all. SS Within measures spread INSIDE each group; where the groups happen to sit is irrelevant to it.
  4. Group 1: (8 − 1) × 2² = 7 × 4 = 28.
  5. Group 2: (10 − 1) × 3² = 9 × 9 = 81.
  6. Group 3: (8 − 1) × 2² = 7 × 4 = 28.
  7. SS Error = 28 + 81 + 28 = 137.
✓ Answer: a. 137.
Why each option is what it is
✓a. Correct. 7(4) + 9(9) + 7(4) = 137.
✗b. What you get from Σ(nᵢ − 1) sᵢ with the squaring forgotten: 7(2) + 9(3) + 7(2) = 55. The variance is s², not s — the whole quantity is a sum of SQUARES.
✗c. What you get from Σ nᵢ sᵢ² with no subtraction: 8(4) + 10(9) + 8(4) = 154. Each group costs you one degree of freedom because its own mean was estimated from its own data.
Carry this forward
Given means, sizes and standard deviations: SS Within = Σ(nᵢ − 1)sᵢ² uses only the sizes and the SDs, and SS Between = Σ nᵢ(x̄ᵢ − overall mean)² uses only the sizes and the means. Check which one the question needs before you start multiplying.
11
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
A study of 24 male subjects undergoing corrective knee surgery classified physical fitness before surgery as below average (n = 8), average (n = 10) or above average (n = 6), and recorded the number of days of physical therapy until fully rehabilitated. The calculated value of the test statistic is:
›
SourcedfSSMSFP-value
Status**********
Error****19.8
Total**1088.0
  • a.11.32
  • b.16.97
  • c.26.97
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
A table with almost everything hidden, and the question wants F. You have one MS, one SS, and the group sizes in the text. That is enough — fill the table backwards.
② Diagnosis
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Get N and k from the TEXT, not the table: N = 8 + 10 + 6 = 24, and k = 3 fitness levels.
  2. Degrees of freedom: df Status = k − 1 = 2, df Error = N − k = 24 − 3 = 21, df Total = 23. Check: 2 + 21 = 23. ✓
  3. Run SS = MS × df backwards on the Error row: SS Error = 19.8 × 21 = 415.8.
  4. SS adds down the column, so SS Status = SS Total − SS Error = 1088.0 − 415.8 = 672.2.
  5. Divide across the Status row: MS Status = 672.2 ÷ 2 = 336.1.
  6. F = MS Status ÷ MS Error = 336.1 ÷ 19.8 = 16.97.
✓ Answer: b. 16.97.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. SS Status ÷ k instead of ÷ (k − 1): 672.2 ÷ 3 = 224.07, and 224.07 ÷ 19.8 = 11.32. One forgotten subtraction, three steps from the end.
✓b. Correct. 672.2 ÷ 2 = 336.1, and 336.1 ÷ 19.8 = 16.97.
✗c. No legitimate route reaches 26.97. It is the right answer with its first digit changed, sitting in the list to catch anyone who half-remembers a number instead of recomputing it. The nearest real near-miss is SS Total ÷ 2 ÷ 19.8 = 27.47 — what you get by forgetting to take SS Error out of SS Total first.
Carry this forward
A table with ** everywhere is still just three rules: SS adds down, MS = SS ÷ df across, F = MS ÷ MS. Running them backwards (SS = MS × df) is the same rules rearranged.
12
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
Referring to the knee-surgery scenario, if the null hypothesis to be tested is H₀: μ_below = μ_average = μ_above, what is the appropriate alternative hypothesis?
›
  • a.Only one of the population means is different from the others
  • b.None of the population means are equal to any other
  • c.At least one of the population means differs
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
The same “what is Hₐ” question as number 5, dressed differently. No arithmetic — just the fixed form of the ANOVA alternative.
② Diagnosis
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. H₀ says all three population means are equal. Hₐ is simply the denial of that: it is NOT true that all three are equal.
  2. Translate the denial into plain English. For “all equal” to be false, you only need ONE mean to sit apart. So: at least one differs.
  3. Check the two words that make an option wrong — “only” and “none”. Both narrow the claim to a particular pattern, and Hₐ covers every pattern that is not “all equal”.
✓ Answer: c. At least one of the population means differs.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. “Only one” is too specific. It excludes the case where two of them differ, which also makes H₀ false — so this alternative does not cover everything that rejecting H₀ would allow.
✗b. This is “all three are different from each other”, the strongest possible claim. Rejecting H₀ never earns you that.
✓c. Correct. It is the exact logical opposite of “all the means are equal”.
Carry this forward
The ANOVA alternative never says “all the means differ” and never names a direction. What it says is “at least one differs” — or, equivalently, “not all are equal”.
13
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
Referring to the knee-surgery scenario, the estimate of the common standard deviation is:
›
SourcedfSSMSF
Status2672.2336.116.97
Error21415.819.8
Total231088.0
  • a.2.15
  • b.3.37
  • c.4.45
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
“The common standard deviation” is the one spread shared by all the groups — the equal-variance assumption says there is only one. It comes straight off the table.
② Diagnosis
Case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. MS Error IS the pooled estimate of the common VARIANCE. That is what the Error row of an ANOVA table estimates: the leftover spread inside the groups, per degree of freedom.
  2. Here MS Error = 19.8, so the common variance is estimated as 19.8.
  3. A standard deviation is the square root of a variance: sₚ = √19.8.
  4. sₚ = 4.4497, which rounds to 4.45.
  5. Sanity check: the pooled standard deviation has to be in the same ballpark as the spread inside the groups. Recovery times varying by about four and a half days around a group mean is exactly what 4.45 describes.
✓ Answer: c. 4.45.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. A square root of something else on the table. There is no route from the Error row to 2.15 — any answer that does not start at MS Error is not estimating the common variance at all.
✗b. The square root of a number near 11.3 — an F value, or a half-remembered mean square. Whatever the route, it does not begin on the ERROR row, which is the only row that estimates the common variance.
✓c. Correct. √(MS Error) = √19.8 = 4.45.
Carry this forward
√(MS Within) is the pooled standard deviation — one number, free from the table, and the one every post-hoc comparison is built on. It is a standard DEVIATION, not a standard error: the standard error of a particular pair is sₚ√(1/nᵢ + 1/nⱼ).
14
Case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Referring to the knee-surgery scenario, making a Type II error in this study is concluding:
›
  • a.mean number of days to recover is NOT the same for all three fitness levels, when in fact they are all the same
  • b.mean number of days to recover IS the same for all three fitness levels, when in fact at least one is different from the others
  • c.mean number of days to recover is different for each of the three fitness levels, when in fact only one is different from the others
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
Which wrong decision is the Type II one? Every option has the same shape — a conclusion, then a “when in fact” clause giving the truth. Your job is to match that pair to the right error name.
② Diagnosis
Case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Fix the definitions before you look at the options. Type I: you REJECT H₀ when it is actually true — a false alarm. Type II: you FAIL to reject H₀ when it is actually false — a missed difference.
  2. Translate both into the language of this study. H₀ here is “all three fitness levels have the same mean recovery time”.
  3. So Type II = you conclude the recovery times are the SAME (you did not reject), when in fact at least one level really is different (H₀ was false).
  4. Now read the options for that exact pattern: conclusion “the same”, truth “at least one differs”.
✓ Answer: b. concluding the means are the same when in fact at least one is different.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. This is the mirror image: concluding there IS a difference when in fact there is none. That is a Type I error — the false alarm.
✓b. Correct. You missed a real difference: failed to reject a false H₀.
✗c. Neither error. The “in fact” half says a real difference exists, and the conclusion says a difference was found — decision and truth agree, so this is a correct rejection, merely over-stated in its wording. No error of either type is possible when the two halves agree.
Carry this forward
Type I = false alarm (rejected a true H₀). Type II = missed it (kept a false H₀). Read the “when in fact” clause FIRST: it tells you the truth, and the truth tells you which error is even possible.
15
Case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
A comparison is made between two experimental groups and a control group. Multiple comparisons use the Bonferroni method with α = 0.10, t** = 2.2426, and the smallest minimum significant difference (MSD) is 17.68. The correct conclusions are:
›
GroupMean scoreStd. dev.
Control7512.6
Group 18418.4
Group 210220.8
  • a.Group 2 has a higher mean score than either the Control or Group 1. The Control and Group 1 are indistinguishable.
  • b.Both treatments have a higher mean score than the Control. The two treatment groups are indistinguishable.
  • c.Group 2 has a higher mean score than the Control. Group 2 and Group 1 are indistinguishable, and Group 1 and the Control are indistinguishable.
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
The hard work has been done for you: the yardstick (MSD = 17.68) is handed over. All that is left is three subtractions and three comparisons. The t** and the α are there to tell you where the MSD came from, not to be used again.
② Diagnosis
Case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. List the pairs. With k = 3 groups there are k(k − 1)/2 = 3 of them: Control vs Group 1, Control vs Group 2, Group 1 vs Group 2.
  2. Group 1 − Control = 84 − 75 = 9. Is 9 bigger than 17.68? No → not distinguishable.
  3. Group 2 − Control = 102 − 75 = 27. Is 27 bigger than 17.68? Yes → a real difference.
  4. Group 2 − Group 1 = 102 − 84 = 18. Is 18 bigger than 17.68? Yes, just → a real difference.
  5. Put the three verdicts into one sentence: Group 2 is above both of the others; Control and Group 1 cannot be told apart.
  6. The standard deviations in the table are not needed — they already went into the MSD. Ignore them, and do not be lured into recomputing anything.
  7. One honest footnote. The question hands you the SMALLEST of the three minimum significant differences, which is the most generous yardstick. With equal group sizes all three MSDs are identical and a single yardstick is exactly right; with unequal sizes the smallest one flatters the closest pair. Use what the question gives you — but notice that Group 2 against Group 1 clears it by only 0.32.
✓ Answer: a. Group 2 beats both; Control and Group 1 are indistinguishable.
Why each option is what it is
✓a. Correct. 27 > 17.68 and 18 > 17.68, but 9 < 17.68.
✗b. Claims Group 1 also beats the Control — but that gap is only 9, well under the yardstick. This is the option you pick if you compare the means by eye instead of against the MSD.
✗c. Gets Group 2 vs Control right and then calls Group 2 and Group 1 indistinguishable. Their gap is 18, which is bigger than 17.68 — only just, and that is exactly why this distractor exists. Do the subtraction; do not estimate it.
Carry this forward
A post-hoc question with the MSD given is arithmetic, not theory: subtract each pair, compare with the yardstick, and watch the pair that lands within a point of it.
17
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
A teacher groups students into three groups to study the impact of other-language skills on learning French (Group 1: no foreign language, good English; Group 2: no foreign language, poor English; Group 3: studied at least one other foreign language). The alternative hypothesis to be tested is:
›
GroupSample sizeMeanStd. dev.
1838.254.6
21232.508.6
31042.307.2
  • a.μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃
  • b.μ₁ ≠ μ₂ ≠ μ₃
  • c.At least two μᵢ differ
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
The table is there for the NEXT question, not this one. This is the Hₐ question again, in symbols this time.
② Diagnosis
Case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Read what is being asked: the ALTERNATIVE hypothesis. Half the marks on this question are lost by answering with H₀.
  2. H₀ is “all three population means are equal”, i.e. μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃.
  3. Hₐ is its denial: not all equal. In symbols there is no tidy way to write that, which is why the correct option is in words.
  4. “At least two μᵢ differ” is the same statement as “at least one mean differs from the others” — if one mean sits apart, then there is a pair that differs.
✓ Answer: c. At least two μᵢ differ.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. This is H₀, printed as a decoy in the Hₐ slot. Whenever one option is the null hypothesis, check which hypothesis the question actually asked for.
✗b. A chain of ≠ signs says every mean differs from every other — the strongest claim available, and not what F tests.
✓c. Correct. Equivalent to “not all the means are equal”.
Carry this forward
Three ways of saying the same correct thing: “not all equal”, “at least one differs”, “at least two differ”. All three are the ANOVA alternative. “All differ” never is.
18
Case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
Referring to the French-class scenario, the pooled estimate of the common standard deviation is equal to:
›
GroupSample sizeMeanStd. dev.
1838.254.6
21232.508.6
31042.307.2
  • a.6.80
  • b.9.17
  • c.7.27
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
Same quantity as question 13 — the one spread shared by all the groups — but now there is no ANOVA table. You have to build MS Within yourself from the summary statistics, and then take its square root.
② Diagnosis
Case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Build SS Within from the group standard deviations: SS Within = Σ (nᵢ − 1) sᵢ².
  2. Group 1: 7 × 4.6² = 7 × 21.16 = 148.12.
  3. Group 2: 11 × 8.6² = 11 × 73.96 = 813.56.
  4. Group 3: 9 × 7.2² = 9 × 51.84 = 466.56.
  5. SS Within = 148.12 + 813.56 + 466.56 = 1428.24.
  6. Degrees of freedom: N = 8 + 12 + 10 = 30, k = 3, so df Within = 30 − 3 = 27.
  7. MS Within = 1428.24 ÷ 27 = 52.90.
  8. sₚ = √52.90 = 7.2731, which rounds to 7.27.
  9. Sanity check: the pooled SD must land between the smallest and largest group SD — between 4.6 and 8.6. 7.27 does. If your answer falls outside that range, you have made an arithmetic error, not a conceptual one.
✓ Answer: c. 7.27.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. The plain average of the three standard deviations: (4.6 + 8.6 + 7.2) ÷ 3 = 6.80. You cannot average standard deviations — you pool variances, weighted by degrees of freedom, and take the root at the end.
✗b. There is no clean route to 9.17 — and you do not need one to rule it out. It is bigger than every group standard deviation in the table, and a pooled value can never land outside the range of the values it pools. The sanity check kills it in two seconds.
✓c. Correct. √(1428.24 ÷ 27) = √52.90 = 7.27.
Carry this forward
Pooling is always: square, weight by (nᵢ − 1), add, divide by N − k, then square-root. The root goes LAST. And the answer always lands between the smallest and largest group SD — use that as a free check.
19
Case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Referring to the French-class scenario, a possible Type I error in this situation is for the teacher to conclude that:
›
  • a.mean test scores are different for all Groups when in fact mean test scores differ only between some Groups
  • b.mean test scores differ between some Groups when in fact they are all the same
  • c.mean test scores are the same for all Groups when in fact at least one of the mean test scores is different from the other Groups
  • d.mean test scores are the same for all Groups when in fact mean test scores are different for all Groups
  • e.a Type I error cannot be defined for more than two means
① Symptom — what the question is really asking
The companion to question 14, with the other error and five options instead of three. Same technique: split every option into “what I concluded” and “what was actually true”.
② Diagnosis
Case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
③ Treatment — the procedure
  1. Type I error = rejecting a TRUE H₀. In this study H₀ is “all three groups have the same mean test score”.
  2. So the truth half must be “they are all the same”, and the conclusion half must be “they differ”.
  3. Scan the “when in fact” clauses first. Only one option has “when in fact they are all the same” — and that is already enough to identify it.
  4. Check its first half: “mean test scores differ between some Groups”. That is a rejection of H₀. Rejection + H₀ actually true = Type I. ✓
✓ Answer: b. concluding that scores differ between some Groups when in fact they are all the same.
Why each option is what it is
✗a. Both halves describe differences existing. H₀ is false in this option, so a Type I error is not even possible here — this is about over-stating a real result, which is a reporting mistake, not a Type I error.
✓b. Correct. A false alarm: H₀ was true and you rejected it anyway.
✗c. Concluded “the same”, truth “at least one differs”. That is a Type II error — the one from question 14.
✗d. Also a Type II error, with the truth half exaggerated to “different for all”. The conclusion half is what decides it: you failed to reject, so it cannot be Type I.
✗e. False. Type I error is defined by the decision about H₀, not by how many means there are. It applies to any hypothesis test.
Carry this forward
Both error questions are answered by the “when in fact” clause: it tells you whether H₀ was true. H₀ true and you rejected → Type I. H₀ false and you did not → Type II.

Practice exam A

Twenty-five questions across all eight case types, at homework difficulty. Answers stay hidden until you commit to one. Afterwards you can retry only the ones you missed.
