Question 1 · case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
A one-way ANOVA compares four teaching methods with 12 students in each. The degrees of freedom for the F test are:
  • a.4 and 48
  • b.3 and 44
  • c.3 and 48
  • d.4 and 44
k = 4 and N = 4 × 12 = 48. df between = k − 1 = 3; df within = N − k = 48 − 4 = 44. Check: 3 + 44 = 47 = N − 1. ✓
The other options
✗a. k and N with no subtraction at all.
✗c. Right numerator, but the denominator forgets to subtract k.
✗d. Right denominator, but the numerator forgets to subtract 1.
🏷️ Both halves cost you something: one for the numerator, k for the denominator.
Question 2 · case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
Three independent samples of 6 observations each have standard deviations 2, 3 and 4. The sum of squares within (error) is:
  • a.45
  • b.29
  • c.145
  • d.174
SS Within = Σ(nᵢ − 1)sᵢ² = 5(4) + 5(9) + 5(16) = 20 + 45 + 80 = 145.
The other options
✗a. 5(2) + 5(3) + 5(4) = 45 — the standard deviations weighted correctly but never squared.
✗b. 4 + 9 + 16 = 29 — the three variances added with no weights at all.
✗d. 6(4) + 6(9) + 6(16) = 174 — nᵢ used instead of nᵢ − 1.
🏷️ Weight by (nᵢ − 1), not nᵢ: each group spends one degree of freedom on its own mean.
Question 3 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
An ANOVA table reports SS Between = 84 with 3 degrees of freedom and SS Within = 240 with 36 degrees of freedom. The F statistic is:
SourcedfSSMSF
Between384??
Within36240?
Total39324
  • a.4.20
  • b.0.35
  • c.0.24
  • d.12.60
MS Between = 84 ÷ 3 = 28. MS Within = 240 ÷ 36 = 6.667. F = 28 ÷ 6.667 = 4.20.
The other options
✗b. 84 ÷ 240 — a ratio of sums of squares instead of mean squares.
✗c. 6.667 ÷ 28 — the ratio inverted.
✗d. 84 ÷ 6.667 — a sum of squares divided by a mean square, mixing the two scales.
🏷️ Divide each SS by its OWN df first; only then take the ratio.
Question 4 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
In a one-way ANOVA with five groups, the alternative hypothesis is:
  • a.μ₁ = μ₂ = μ₃ = μ₄ = μ₅
  • b.all five population means are different from one another
  • c.at least one population mean differs from the others
  • d.the five sample means are not all equal
Hₐ is the flat denial of “all the population means are equal”, which is “at least one differs”. It makes no claim about direction, about which group, or about how many.
The other options
✗a. That is H₀.
✗b. The strongest possible claim, and far more than rejecting H₀ earns you.
✗d. Hypotheses are always about POPULATION means. Sample means are what you measured; they are never in doubt and never in a hypothesis.
🏷️ Two checks on any Hₐ option: is it about the population, and does it say “at least one”?
Question 5 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Three groups have standard deviations 3.1, 4.0 and 5.9, and the data look approximately Normal with no outliers. Using the rule of thumb from the course, is the ANOVA appropriate?
  • a.Yes
  • b.No
  • c.Only if the group sizes are equal
  • d.Not enough information to tell
The rule of thumb: the largest standard deviation must be no more than twice the smallest. Twice 3.1 is 6.2, and the largest is 5.9, which is below it (5.9 ÷ 3.1 = 1.90). Normality is given, so the ANOVA is appropriate.
The other options
✗b. This is what you answer if you compare 5.9 with 3.1 and simply feel they are far apart. The rule is a factor of two, and 1.90 is inside it.
✗c. Equal group sizes make the F test more robust, but they are not an assumption of ANOVA and are not required here.
✗d. You have the three standard deviations and a statement about shape — that is everything the rule of thumb needs.
🏷️ Largest s ÷ smallest s. At most 2 and you are fine; above 2 and you are not.
Question 6 · case type 6 · Effect size: R² (eta-squared)
An ANOVA gives SS Between = 150 and SS Within = 450. The value of R² (eta-squared) is:
  • a.0.33
  • b.0.25
  • c.0.75
  • d.3.00
R² = SS Between ÷ SS TOTAL, and SS Total = 150 + 450 = 600. R² = 150 ÷ 600 = 0.25: the factor accounts for a quarter of the total spread.
The other options
✗a. 150 ÷ 450 — SS Between over SS WITHIN. The denominator of R² is always the total.
✗c. 450 ÷ 600 — the share belonging to the noise, not to the factor.
✗d. 450 ÷ 150 — a ratio bigger than 1, which no proportion can be.
🏷️ R² is a proportion, so it must land between 0 and 1, and its denominator is SS Total.
Question 7 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
A researcher concludes that four fertilisers produce different mean yields, when in truth all four fertilisers produce the same mean yield. This is:
  • a.a correct decision
  • b.a Type II error
  • c.a Type I error
  • d.not an error, only low power
H₀ (all means equal) was TRUE, and the researcher rejected it. Rejecting a true null is a Type I error — a false alarm, with probability α.
The other options
✗a. The conclusion contradicts the truth, so it cannot be correct.
✗b. A Type II error is the opposite: failing to reject a FALSE null.
✗d. Power is about detecting real differences. Here there was nothing to detect.
🏷️ Read the “when in truth…” half first: it tells you whether H₀ was true, and that decides which error is even possible.
Question 8 · case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
After a significant F with five groups, how many pairwise comparisons are there?
  • a.4
  • b.5
  • c.10
  • d.20
k(k − 1)/2 = 5 × 4 ÷ 2 = 10. Each unordered pair is counted once.
The other options
✗a. k − 1, the between degrees of freedom — a different quantity entirely.
✗b. The number of groups, not the number of pairs.
✗d. 5 × 4 = 20 counts every pair twice: group 1 vs 2 and group 2 vs 1 are one comparison.
🏷️ Divide by 2, because a pair is a pair whichever way round you write it.
Question 9 · case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
A Bonferroni correction is applied to all the pairwise comparisons among FIVE groups at an overall α = .05. The alpha used for each individual test is:
  • a..005
  • b..01
  • c..05
  • d..50
Bonferroni divides the overall alpha by the number of tests: .05 ÷ 10 = .005.
The other options
✗b. .05 ÷ 5 — divided by the number of GROUPS instead of the number of comparisons.
✗c. No correction at all, which is the problem Bonferroni exists to solve.
✗d. .05 × 10 — multiplied rather than divided, giving an alpha above every sensible value and making the test easier instead of harder.
🏷️ The correction always makes each test STRICTER, so the per-test alpha must come out smaller than the overall one.
Question 10 · case type 1 · Name the design
A one-way ANOVA is run on exactly two groups, and a two-sample t test is run on the same data. Which statement is true?
  • a.they can reach different conclusions, because ANOVA is two-sided and the t test is one-sided
  • b.F = t², so the two tests give identical p-values and the same conclusion
  • c.the ANOVA is invalid, because it needs at least three groups
  • d.the t test is invalid, because the data have more than one group
With two groups the two tests are algebraically the same test: F = t², and the p-values match exactly. That identity is why ANOVA is called the extension of the t test.
The other options
✗a. A two-sided t test and the F test agree exactly; the squaring is what removes the sign, not what changes the answer.
✗c. ANOVA handles two groups perfectly well. It is simply not more informative than a t test there.
✗d. Comparing two groups is exactly what a two-sample t test is for.
🏷️ F = t² for two groups, against the pooled t test, and the p-values are identical — which is why ANOVA is called the extension of the t test.
Question 11 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
An ANOVA table shows MS Within = 12.5 with 36 degrees of freedom within. SS Within is:
  • a.2.88
  • b.450
  • c.12.5
  • d.437.5
MS = SS ÷ df, so SS = MS × df = 12.5 × 36 = 450. The same rule, run backwards.
The other options
✗a. 36 ÷ 12.5 — the division the wrong way round.
✗c. MS copied as if it were SS. They are only equal when df = 1.
✗d. 12.5 × 35 — the right multiplication, with the within df accidentally reduced by one. Nothing in the table asks for that extra subtraction.
🏷️ Every backwards table question is one of the three forward rules rearranged.
Question 12 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
A one-way ANOVA produces F = 1.08 with p = 0.37. The correct conclusion at α = .05 is:
  • a.there is enough evidence to conclude that the population means are all equal
  • b.at least one population mean differs from the others
  • c.the sample means are all equal
  • d.there is not enough evidence that the population means differ
p = 0.37 is larger than α, so H₀ is not rejected. Failing to reject is never proof that H₀ is true — it means the data did not supply enough evidence against it.
The other options
✗a. Too strong. You never accept H₀; absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.
✗b. That is the conclusion for a SMALL p-value.
✗c. The sample means are almost certainly not equal — they just are not far enough apart to be convincing. Hypotheses are never about the sample anyway.
🏷️ A large p-value buys you a careful sentence, never a confident one.
Question 13 · case type 1 · Name the design
Shoppers are randomly assigned to hear one of three types of background music, and the amount they spend is recorded. In this study:
  • a.the factor is the amount spent with three levels, and the dependent variable is the type of music
  • b.the dependent variable is the type of music, and it is quantitative with three levels
  • c.the factor is the type of music with three levels, and the dependent variable is the amount spent
  • d.there are three factors, one per type of music, and one dependent variable
The dependent variable is what was MEASURED on each person and is quantitative: amount spent. The factor is the qualitative variable that says which group you are in: type of music, with three levels (so k = 3).
The other options
✗a. The factor and the dependent variable swapped.
✗b. Type of music is qualitative, and it is the grouping variable, not the outcome.
✗d. One factor with three levels — not three factors. “One-way” means exactly one factor.
🏷️ Find the quantitative measurement first: that is always the dependent variable. Whatever is left and categorical is the factor.
Question 14 · case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
Four groups have sizes 7, 9, 10 and 14. The within-groups degrees of freedom are:
  • a.40
  • b.39
  • c.36
  • d.3
N = 7 + 9 + 10 + 14 = 40 and k = 4, so df Within = N − k = 40 − 4 = 36.
The other options
✗a. N itself, with nothing subtracted.
✗b. N − 1, which is the TOTAL df, not the within df.
✗d. k − 1, which is the BETWEEN df.
🏷️ Unequal group sizes change nothing: add them up to get N, then subtract k.
Question 15 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
An ANOVA table reports MS Within = 16.0. The pooled estimate of the common standard deviation is:
  • a.4.0
  • b.16.0
  • c.256.0
  • d.8.0
MS Within estimates the common VARIANCE, so the common standard deviation is its square root: √16.0 = 4.0.
The other options
✗b. That is the variance, not the standard deviation.
✗c. 16² — squared instead of square-rooted.
✗d. 16 ÷ 2, which is not how a square root works.
🏷️ MS Within is a variance. Anything called a standard deviation is its square root.
Question 16 · case type 6 · Effect size: R² (eta-squared)
An ANOVA on a large sample gives p < .001 and R² = .04. The best summary is:
  • a.a large and important effect
  • b.the result must be a calculation error, since p is small but R² is not
  • c.the groups do not really differ
  • d.a difference that is almost certainly real, but small
The p-value and R² answer different questions. p says whether the difference is bigger than chance; R² says how much of the spread the factor accounts for. A big sample can make a tiny effect statistically significant.
The other options
✗a. R² = .04 is about 4% of the variance — small by any standard.
✗b. There is no contradiction: significance and size are independent questions, which is exactly why both get reported.
✗c. p < .001 says they do differ.
🏷️ Significant answers “is it real?”. R² answers “is it big?”. Never let one answer the other’s question.
Question 17 · case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
Post-hoc comparisons give a minimum significant difference of 6.5. The group means are A = 20, B = 25 and C = 32. Which pairs differ?
  • a.all three pairs
  • b.A and C, and B and C
  • c.A and B only
  • d.none of the pairs
B − A = 5 (below 6.5, not distinguishable). C − A = 12 (above 6.5, differ). C − B = 7 (above 6.5, differ). So C stands apart from both; A and B do not.
The other options
✗a. A and B are only 5 apart, which is under the yardstick.
✗c. The one pair that is NOT different.
✗d. Two of the three gaps clear 6.5 comfortably.
🏷️ Do all three subtractions and compare each with the MSD. Never decide by how far apart the means look.
Question 18 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
A significant F in a one-way ANOVA with four groups allows you to conclude that:
  • a.every group mean differs from every other
  • b.the four population means are not all equal
  • c.the group with the highest sample mean has the highest population mean
  • d.the factor caused the difference
A significant F rejects “all the population means are equal” and nothing more. Which means differ is a separate, post-hoc question.
The other options
✗a. That would need every pairwise comparison to be significant, which F never tests.
✗c. Ranking the groups needs post-hoc comparisons; sample order alone is not evidence.
✗d. Causality comes from the DESIGN — manipulation and random assignment — never from the size of F.
🏷️ A significant F is modest by nature: at least one, somewhere, in the population.
Question 19 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Students’ exam scores are compared across three degree programmes they had already chosen for themselves. The ANOVA gives F = 9.4, p < .001. You may conclude that:
  • a.the programme causes the difference in population mean scores
  • b.nothing, because ANOVA cannot be used on observational data
  • c.the population means differ, but not necessarily because of the programme
  • d.students should switch to the highest-scoring programme
The analysis is valid and the difference is real, but students chose their own programmes. Without manipulation and random assignment the groups may differ in many other ways, so no causal claim follows however large F is.
The other options
✗a. Self-selected groups make this unsupportable.
✗b. ANOVA is perfectly valid on observational data; it is the CAUSAL interpretation that is not.
✗d. Advice, not a statistical conclusion, and it rests on the causal claim just ruled out.
🏷️ Ask two questions: was the factor manipulated, and were people randomly assigned? Both yes → causal claim allowed. Otherwise not.
Question 20 · case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
Three groups of 10 have means 12, 15 and 18; the overall mean is 15. SS Between is:
  • a.180
  • b.18
  • c.90
  • d.60
SS Between = Σ nᵢ(x̄ᵢ − overall mean)² = 10(12 − 15)² + 10(15 − 15)² + 10(18 − 15)² = 10(9) + 0 + 10(9) = 180.
The other options
✗b. (9 + 0 + 9) with the group sizes left out — the weighting by group size is the whole point of the formula.
✗c. 180 ÷ 2, which is MS Between, not SS Between.
✗d. 10|12 − 15| + 0 + 10|18 − 15| = 60 — the deviations taken in absolute value and never squared. The formula asks for squares, not absolute values.
🏷️ Every squared deviation of a group mean is multiplied by that group’s size.
Question 21 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
In an ANOVA table, which entry estimates the common variance of the populations?
  • a.SS Within
  • b.MS Within
  • c.MS Between
  • d.SS Total ÷ N
MS Within is the pooled within-group variance: the leftover spread divided by its own degrees of freedom. Under the equal-variance assumption it estimates the single common population variance.
The other options
✗a. A sum, not a mean: it still has to be divided by its df.
✗c. MS Between estimates the common variance only when H₀ is TRUE; when H₀ is false it is inflated by the real differences. That is precisely why F compares the two.
✗d. Close to the overall variance of all the scores, which ignores the grouping altogether.
🏷️ MS Within is the noise estimate, and it is the only one that is trustworthy whether or not H₀ holds.
Question 22 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
Using an F table, you reject H₀ when:
  • a.the observed F is smaller than the critical value
  • b.the observed F is larger than the critical value
  • c.the observed F is close to 1
  • d.the observed F is negative
Large F means the group means are further apart than the within-group noise explains, so the rejection region is the upper tail: reject when observed F exceeds the critical value (equivalently, when p < α).
The other options
✗a. That is the region where the data look like H₀ is true.
✗c. F near 1 is exactly what H₀ predicts.
✗d. F is a ratio of two mean squares, both of which are sums of squares divided by positive df, so F can never be negative.
🏷️ The F test is one-tailed on the right even though Hₐ has no direction — squaring already removed the signs.
Question 23 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
A study of three training programmes does not reject H₀. Which statement is correct?
  • a.the three programmes are equally effective
  • b.the probability that this conclusion is a mistake is α
  • c.if one programme really is better, the study has made a Type II error
  • d.the result proves that H₀ is true
Failing to reject leaves two possibilities open: H₀ is true, or H₀ is false and the study missed it. The second case is precisely a Type II error. Nothing here is proved, and α is the risk attached to REJECTING, not to failing to reject.
The other options
✗a. “No evidence of a difference” is not “evidence of no difference”.
✗b. α is the probability of a Type I error, which only arises when you reject. The risk attached to this decision is β.
✗d. A hypothesis test never proves a hypothesis; it only fails to find evidence against it.
🏷️ A non-significant result is an open verdict, not an acquittal.
Question 24 · case type 6 · Effect size: R² (eta-squared)
An ANOVA reports SS Between = 240, SS Within = 160, with 2 and 27 degrees of freedom. R² is:
SourcedfSSMSF
Between224012020.25
Within271605.93
Total29400
  • a.0.40
  • b.1.50
  • c.0.60
  • d.0.67
SS Total = 240 + 160 = 400, so R² = 240 ÷ 400 = 0.60. Sixty per cent of the total spread is accounted for by the factor.
The other options
✗a. 160 ÷ 400 — the share left to the noise.
✗b. 240 ÷ 160 — not a proportion at all, as it exceeds 1.
✗d. 160 ÷ 240 — the two non-total rows divided by each other instead of by SS Total.
🏷️ R² uses the SS column only, and its denominator is the bottom row.
Question 25 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
Which sentence correctly reports a significant one-way ANOVA on three diets?
  • a.The three sample means were different, F = 6.2, p = .004.
  • b.All three diets differed from one another, F = 6.2, p = .004.
  • c.Diet A caused the highest weight loss, F = 6.2, p = .004.
  • d.Mean weight loss differed across the three diets, F(2, 57) = 6.2, p = .004.
A good report is about the POPULATION, claims only “not all equal”, and carries the pair of degrees of freedom with F so the reader can check it.
The other options
✗a. Sample means differ by definition; the claim has to be about the population.
✗b. Over-claims: a significant F never says all pairs differ.
✗c. A causal claim, and about one specific group — neither follows from F.
🏷️ F always travels with both degrees of freedom: F(df between, df within).

Practice exam B

A second, independent set. Save it for a few days after exam A — spacing the two out is worth more than doing both in one sitting.

0 of 25 answered
Question 1 · case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
A study compares six brands of battery with 5 batteries tested per brand. The degrees of freedom reported with the F statistic are:
  • a.6 and 30
  • b.5 and 30
  • c.5 and 24
  • d.6 and 24
k = 6 and N = 6 × 5 = 30. df between = k − 1 = 5; df within = N − k = 30 − 6 = 24. Check: 5 + 24 = 29 = N − 1. ✓
The other options
✗a. Neither subtraction done.
✗b. Numerator right, denominator left as N.
✗d. Denominator right, numerator left as k.
🏷️ Do the addition check — if your two df do not add to N − 1, one of them is wrong.
Question 2 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
Complete the table: what is MS Within?
SourcedfSSMSF
Between3126.042.0?
Within28210.0?
Total31336.0
  • a.210.0
  • b.42.0
  • c.7.5
  • d.5.6
MS = SS ÷ df on the same row: 210.0 ÷ 28 = 7.5. (And then F = 42.0 ÷ 7.5 = 5.6.)
The other options
✗a. SS Within copied without dividing.
✗b. MS Between, read off the wrong row.
✗d. That is the F statistic, the step after this one.
🏷️ Never cross rows. MS on a row uses only that row’s SS and that row’s df.
Question 3 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
An ANOVA on four fertilisers gives F = 3.9 with p = .013. At α = .01 the correct decision is:
  • a.reject H₀, because F is greater than 1
  • b.do not reject H₀, because p is greater than α
  • c.reject H₀, because p is small
  • d.accept H₀, because the means are equal
Compare p with the α you were given, not with .05 out of habit: .013 > .01, so H₀ is not rejected at this level. The same result WOULD be significant at α = .05.
The other options
✗a. F greater than 1 is not a decision rule — F is usually above 1 even when H₀ is true.
✗c. “Small” is relative to α, and here .013 is not small enough.
✗d. You never accept H₀, and the sample means are certainly not equal.
🏷️ Read the α the question gives you. Changing α changes the decision, and exams exploit that.
Question 4 · case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
Two groups of 11 and one group of 9 have standard deviations 3, 4 and 5 respectively. SS Within is:
  • a.110
  • b.450
  • c.500
  • d.50
SS Within = Σ(nᵢ − 1)sᵢ² = 10(9) + 10(16) + 8(25) = 90 + 160 + 200 = 450.
The other options
✗a. 10(3) + 10(4) + 8(5) = 110 — weighted correctly, but the standard deviations were never squared.
✗c. 11(9) + 11(16) + 9(25) = 500 — nᵢ used instead of nᵢ − 1.
✗d. 9 + 16 + 25 = 50 — the variances added with no weights at all.
🏷️ Unequal group sizes only change the weights; the formula is unchanged.
Question 5 · case type 1 · Name the design
Patients are randomly assigned to one of three painkillers and their pain is rated on a 0–100 scale. How many factors and levels are there?
  • a.three factors, each with one level
  • b.one factor with 100 levels
  • c.three factors and one dependent variable
  • d.one factor with three levels
The factor is “which painkiller”, a single qualitative variable, and its levels are the three drugs, so k = 3. The pain rating is the quantitative dependent variable.
The other options
✗a. Levels of one factor, mistaken for separate factors.
✗b. The 0–100 scale is the dependent variable’s range, not levels of a factor.
✗c. Same confusion between a factor and its levels.
🏷️ “One-way” tells you there is exactly one factor before you read anything else.
Question 6 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the one-way ANOVA?
  • a.the population scores are approximately Normally distributed
  • b.the groups contain equal numbers of observations
  • c.the populations have the same variance
  • d.the observations are independent
The three assumptions are Normality, equal population variances, and independence. Equal group SIZES are not required — they make the test more robust to unequal variances, but ANOVA handles unbalanced designs routinely.
The other options
✗a. An assumption.
✗c. An assumption — the one checked with the “largest s ≤ 2 × smallest s” rule.
✗d. An assumption, and the one that is secured by the design rather than checked in the data.
🏷️ Three assumptions, and group size is not one of them.
Question 7 · case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
Why can a researcher not simply run every pairwise t test at α = .05 after an ANOVA?
  • a.because the family-wise false-positive rate rises with the number of tests
  • b.because t tests cannot be used on more than two groups
  • c.because the pooled standard deviation is unknown
  • d.because the F test has already used up the data
Each test carries its own 5% risk. Across several tests, the chance of at least one false alarm climbs well above 5% — with three tests it is about 14%. Bonferroni and Tukey hold that family-wise rate down.
The other options
✗b. A t test compares exactly two groups, which is what a pairwise comparison is.
✗c. It is known: sₚ = √(MS Within), straight from the ANOVA table.
✗d. Not a statistical principle — post-hoc tests use the same data by design.
🏷️ The problem is the family-wise error rate, not the t test itself.
Question 8 · case type 6 · Effect size: R² (eta-squared)
In a one-way ANOVA, R² (eta-squared) tells you:
  • a.whether the difference between the means is statistically significant
  • b.the probability that H₀ is true
  • c.the share of the total variation in the scores accounted for by the factor
  • d.the average difference between the group means
R² = SS Between ÷ SS Total: of all the spread in the dependent variable, this is the share attributable to which group someone is in.
The other options
✗a. That is what the p-value does.
✗b. No statistic gives the probability that H₀ is true; a p-value is computed ASSUMING H₀ is true.
✗d. R² is a proportion of variance, not a difference in the units of the outcome.
🏷️ Significance and effect size are separate questions, answered by separate numbers.
Question 9 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
An ANOVA with three groups reports MS Between = 48 and F = 6.0. MS Within is:
  • a.288
  • b.54
  • c.42
  • d.8
F = MS Between ÷ MS Within, so MS Within = MS Between ÷ F = 48 ÷ 6.0 = 8.
The other options
✗a. 48 × 6 — multiplied instead of divided.
✗b. 48 + 6.
✗c. 48 − 6.
🏷️ Any one of F, MS Between and MS Within can be recovered from the other two.
Question 10 · case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
An ANOVA table shows df Between = 4 and df Total = 49. How many groups and how many observations are there?
  • a.5 groups, 50 observations
  • b.4 groups, 49 observations
  • c.5 groups, 49 observations
  • d.4 groups, 50 observations
df Between = k − 1 = 4, so k = 5. df Total = N − 1 = 49, so N = 50. (Check: df Within = N − k = 45, and 4 + 45 = 49. ✓)
The other options
✗b. The two df copied as the counts, with no reversal of the subtraction.
✗c. k reversed correctly, N not.
✗d. N reversed correctly, k not.
🏷️ Reading a table backwards is the same two rules with the subtraction undone.
Question 11 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Which error does testing more participants make less likely, and what is its probability called?
  • a.a Type I error, probability α
  • b.a Type II error, probability β
  • c.both, because α and β are the same quantity
  • d.neither, because sample size affects only the effect size
A larger sample gives a more precise estimate of the means, so a real difference is more likely to be detected: the chance of MISSING it (β, the Type II error) falls, and power = 1 − β rises. α does not move, because the researcher sets it.
The other options
✗a. α is chosen by the researcher before the data arrive; collecting more people does not change it.
✗c. They are different quantities, attached to opposite decisions: α to rejecting, β to failing to reject.
✗d. The effect size is a property of the populations and does not depend on how many people you test — but your ability to detect it does.
🏷️ More data buys you power (1 − β). It does not buy you a smaller α; you fix that yourself.
Question 12 · case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
Four groups of 5 have means 10, 12, 14 and 16, and the overall mean is 13. SS Between is:
  • a.20
  • b.100
  • c.25
  • d.50
SS Between = Σ nᵢ(x̄ᵢ − overall)² = 5(9) + 5(1) + 5(1) + 5(9) = 45 + 5 + 5 + 45 = 100.
The other options
✗a. (9 + 1 + 1 + 9) = 20 with the group sizes omitted.
✗c. 100 ÷ 4 — divided by the number of GROUPS. MS Between would be 100 ÷ 3 = 33.3 anyway, and the question asked for a sum of squares, not a mean square.
✗d. Half the terms included, or deviations not squared.
🏷️ Deviations are squared first, then multiplied by the group size, then added.
Question 13 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
The null hypothesis of a one-way ANOVA with k groups is:
  • a.μ₁ = μ₂ = … = μₖ
  • b.x̄₁ = x̄₂ = … = x̄ₖ
  • c.at least one μᵢ differs from the others
  • d.σ₁ = σ₂ = … = σₖ
H₀ says all the POPULATION means are equal. That is the claim F puts on trial.
The other options
✗b. Sample means, which are observed, not hypothesised.
✗c. That is Hₐ.
✗d. Equal population variances is an ASSUMPTION of the test, not the hypothesis it tests — a neat trap.
🏷️ Assumption and hypothesis are different jobs: one must hold for the test to work, the other is what the test decides about.
Question 14 · case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
Post-hoc comparisons on four groups are run with Bonferroni at an overall α = .05. The per-comparison alpha is:
  • a..0125
  • b..0167
  • c..0083
  • d..05
Four groups give k(k − 1)/2 = 6 pairs, so each test runs at .05 ÷ 6 = .0083.
The other options
✗a. .05 ÷ 4 — divided by the number of groups rather than the number of pairs.
✗b. .05 ÷ 3 — divided by k − 1, the between degrees of freedom. The df and the number of comparisons are different counts.
✗d. No correction applied at all.
🏷️ Count the PAIRS first; the number of groups is not the number of tests.
Question 15 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
Using the table below, the estimate of the common standard deviation is:
SourcedfSSMSF
Between2182.091.011.6
Within33259.057.85
Total35441.05
  • a.7.85
  • b.2.80
  • c.9.54
  • d.61.62
The common variance is estimated by MS Within = 7.85, so the common standard deviation is √7.85 = 2.80.
The other options
✗a. That is the variance, before the square root.
✗c. √91.0 — the square root of the wrong row.
✗d. 7.85² — squared instead of rooted.
🏷️ Always the ERROR row, always the square root, always last.
Question 16 · case type 1 · Name the design
Which study would be analysed with a one-way ANOVA rather than a two-sample t test?
  • a.comparing mean reaction time for men and women
  • b.comparing mean reaction time across three age bands
  • c.comparing the proportion of passes in two classes
  • d.comparing each person’s score before and after training
ANOVA is for a quantitative outcome compared across THREE OR MORE groups. Three age bands with reaction time measured on each person is exactly that.
The other options
✗a. Two groups — a two-sample t test does it.
✗c. Proportions, not means: the wrong kind of dependent variable.
✗d. The same people measured twice: a paired design, which one-way ANOVA does not cover.
🏷️ Quantitative outcome + one qualitative factor + three or more independent groups = one-way ANOVA.
Question 17 · case type 6 · Effect size: R² (eta-squared)
An ANOVA gives SS Total = 800 and SS Within = 500. R² is:
  • a.0.625
  • b.0.375
  • c.0.60
  • d.1.60
SS Between = 800 − 500 = 300, so R² = 300 ÷ 800 = 0.375.
The other options
✗a. 500 ÷ 800 — the proportion left unexplained, which is 1 − R².
✗c. 300 ÷ 500 — SS Between over SS WITHIN, which is not R².
✗d. 800 ÷ 500 — above 1, so it cannot be a proportion at all.
🏷️ When only two of the three sums of squares are given, the third is one subtraction away.
Question 18 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
Which statement about the F statistic is TRUE?
  • a.F can be negative when the group means are below the overall mean
  • b.F is the ratio of SS Between to SS Within
  • c.F close to 0 is strong evidence against H₀
  • d.F is expected to be about 1 when H₀ is true
Both mean squares estimate the same common variance when H₀ is true, so their ratio is around 1. Evidence against H₀ is F comfortably ABOVE 1.
The other options
✗a. Every term in both mean squares is a square divided by positive df, so F ≥ 0 always.
✗b. A ratio of MEAN squares. Sums of squares are not comparable until each is divided by its own df.
✗c. F near 0 means the group means are closer together than noise alone would predict — the opposite of evidence against H₀.
🏷️ Anchor on F ≈ 1 under H₀. Every true/false statement about F can be checked against it.
Question 19 · case type 8 · What you may conclude — and which error you may have made
Three fertilisers are randomly assigned to 60 identical plots, and yields are compared. F is significant. The strongest justified conclusion is:
  • a.the fertilisers are associated with different yields, but no causal claim is possible
  • b.the fertiliser affects yield, and at least one fertiliser differs from the others
  • c.every fertiliser produces a different yield
  • d.the highest-yielding fertiliser should be adopted nationally
The factor was manipulated by the researcher AND the plots were randomly assigned, so this is a true experiment and a causal claim IS allowed. The claim itself stays modest: at least one differs.
The other options
✗a. Too cautious: random assignment plus manipulation is exactly what licenses causality.
✗c. Too strong: a significant F never says all pairs differ.
✗d. A policy recommendation, not a statistical conclusion — and it needs post-hoc tests to identify the best one.
🏷️ Causality is decided by the design, not the p-value. Manipulated + randomly assigned → you may say “affects”.
Question 20 · case type 2 · Degrees of freedom
In a one-way ANOVA, which pair of degrees of freedom is used to look up the critical F?
  • a.(N − 1, N − k)
  • b.(k, N − k)
  • c.(k − 1, N − k)
  • d.(N − k, k − 1)
The numerator df comes first: (df between, df within) = (k − 1, N − k).
The other options
✗a. Total df on top — a common slip when the table prints three df.
✗b. Numerator missing its subtraction.
✗d. The right two numbers in the wrong ORDER. F tables are not symmetric, so the order changes the critical value.
🏷️ Numerator first, always: between on top, within underneath, in that order.
Question 21 · case type 3 · Build the sums of squares
An ANOVA has SS Between = 310 and SS Total = 1240. SS Within is:
  • a.1550
  • b.4.0
  • c.930
  • d.0.25
Sums of squares add down the column: SS Within = SS Total − SS Between = 1240 − 310 = 930.
The other options
✗a. The two added instead of subtracted.
✗b. 1240 ÷ 310 — a ratio, not a sum of squares.
✗d. 310 ÷ 1240 — that is R², not SS Within.
🏷️ Given any two of the three sums of squares, the third is one line of arithmetic.
Question 22 · case type 7 · After the test: which pairs differ?
A significant F is followed by post-hoc tests. Which quantity do those tests use as their estimate of spread?
  • a.the standard deviation of the largest group
  • b.the standard deviation of all the scores pooled together, ignoring groups
  • c.SS Within
  • d.the pooled standard deviation sₚ = √(MS Within), with df = df Within
Post-hoc comparisons borrow strength from the whole study: they use the pooled within-group estimate from the ANOVA table, with its degrees of freedom. That pooled error term uses all the data, so it is a more precise estimate of spread than any single pair could supply — though the family-wise correction still makes each comparison stricter than an uncorrected t test would be.
The other options
✗a. Using one group throws away the information in the others.
✗b. Ignoring groups mixes the between-group differences back into the noise estimate.
✗c. A sum, not yet divided by its df.
🏷️ Post-hoc tests reuse the ANOVA’s own error term — that is the whole reason the ANOVA comes first.
Question 23 · case type 4 · Fill in the ANOVA table
Fill in the blanks: with SS Between = 64, df Between = 2, and MS Within = 4, the F statistic is:
SourcedfSSMSF
Between264??
Within****4
Total****
  • a.8.0
  • b.16.0
  • c.32.0
  • d.2.0
MS Between = 64 ÷ 2 = 32, and F = 32 ÷ 4 = 8.0.
The other options
✗b. 64 ÷ 4 — the SS divided by the mean square, skipping the df step.
✗c. That is MS Between, one step short of F.
✗d. 4 ÷ 2 — MS Within divided by df Between. Both numbers are on the table; neither division is a step on the way to F.
🏷️ Two moves, in order: SS ÷ df to get MS, then MS ÷ MS to get F.
Question 24 · case type 6 · Effect size: R² (eta-squared)
Two studies report the same R² = .30, but study 1 has p = .002 and study 2 has p = .21. The most likely explanation is:
  • a.study 2 made an arithmetic error
  • b.study 2 has a much smaller sample
  • c.study 2 has a larger effect
  • d.R² cannot be compared across studies
R² measures the size of the effect; the p-value also depends on sample size. The same effect size in a small sample produces a larger p-value, because there is less evidence.
The other options
✗a. There is no contradiction to explain away.
✗c. Equal R² means equal effect size.
✗d. R² is a proportion of variance and is designed to be comparable.
🏷️ p depends on effect size AND sample size. R² depends only on effect size.
Question 25 · case type 5 · Test it: F, the table, the decision
An ANOVA on four groups gives F(3, 56) = 2.30. The critical value at α = .05 is 2.77. You should:
  • a.reject H₀, because F is greater than 1
  • b.reject H₀, because 2.30 is close to 2.77
  • c.not reject H₀, because 2.30 is smaller than the critical value
  • d.not reject H₀, because F must exceed 4 to be significant
The decision rule is a comparison with the critical value: 2.30 < 2.77, so the observed F falls outside the rejection region and H₀ stands.
The other options
✗a. F above 1 is ordinary; it is not a rejection rule.
✗b. “Close” is not a decision. The boundary is the boundary.
✗d. There is no universal threshold — the critical value depends entirely on the two degrees of freedom and on α.
🏷️ Compare with the critical value the question gives you, and do not negotiate with the boundary.
